# Reading Log 2024

## Summary
Twenty books this year, a shade fewer than 2023 and comfortably past the fifteen I set as a floor in January. I kept the list in a small notebook and wrote a line or two the day I finished each one, which turns the end-of-year review into a matter of reading back rather than remembering. The mix ran about two thirds fiction and a third non-fiction, and the fiction leaned toward the long and the slow rather than anything quick. Most of the reading happened on the train, forty minutes each way, and a good chunk of it on the sofa on wet Sundays. I gave up on one book about a third in and felt fine about it. The point of the log is not the count but the record of what actually held my attention. I read a little faster than last year without trying to, which I put down to the train habit rather than any improvement in me. The longest book was Austerlitz and the shortest a slim non-fiction thing I finished in two sittings. I bought fewer books than I read, which is the first time that has been true, mostly because the library near the station has a good shelf and I started using it properly. The one thing I want more of next year is translated fiction, which barely featured at all this time.

## Finished
I started the year with Station Eleven by Emily St John Mandel, which I had put off for years and then read in a week. The Dispossessed by Ursula K. Le Guin came next and was the best thing I read all year, slow at the start and then impossible to put down. Austerlitz by W. G. Sebald took most of March and demanded quiet, but it was worth every patient page. I read The Odyssey in Emily Wilson's translation across April and May, a few books at a time, and the plain language made it feel like a story rather than a monument. Wolf Hall by Hilary Mantel gripped me through the early summer, dense with voices and politics. In August I took The Sea, The Sea by Iris Murdoch on holiday and finished it in the sun, strange and long and memorable. The Sellout by Paul Beatty was the funniest thing of the year and I laughed out loud on the train more than once. Gilead by Marilynne Robinson closed the year in December, quiet and slow and completely worth the wait. A couple of slighter books filled the gaps between the big ones. There was a short non-fiction book about maps that I enjoyed far more than I expected, and a crime novel that was perfect for a wet weekend and forgotten by the Monday. I read two books by the same author for the first time, which was accidental rather than planned. The Odyssey was the one I thought about most after finishing, partly for the plainness of the language and partly for how much of it came back to me from school.

## Notes
The one I abandoned was a long history that I had been meaning to read for a decade and finally admitted I was not going to finish; it went back to the shelf without guilt. I noticed this year that I read better in the morning than late at night, when the same page takes three passes to stick. Next year I want more in translation and at least one book I have dodged for years, and I want to reread The Dispossessed slowly with a pencil, since it seems to reward a second pass even more than the first. I also want to stop buying books faster than I read them, since the to-read shelf keeps growing and the newest arrival always wins over the one that has waited a year. Keeping the notebook was the best decision of the year and I will do the same again, one line per book, no pressure to write more.
